questions.q: Why does the lesson recommend always passing `timeout=` to a requests.get() or requests.post() call?
options: It converts the response into JSON automatically
It is required syntax and the call will raise a SyntaxError without it
Without it, a hung request with no response can stall a script indefinitely
It automatically retries failed requests
questions.explain: A timeout ensures a request that never gets a response doesn't block the script forever; it is a defensive habit, not a required parameter.

questions.q: What is the OAuth2 client credentials grant used for, as described in this lesson?
options: Automatically paginating through API results
Machine-to-machine authentication with no human user involved, trading a client ID and secret for a short-lived access token
Encrypting the response body of every API call
Letting a human user log in with a username and password through a browser redirect
questions.explain: The client credentials grant is specifically the OAuth2 flow for app-to-app authentication without a human user, used by most security platform APIs for automation.

questions.q: In the pagination example, what bug does looping on `next_page_token` guard against?
options: The access token expiring mid-request
The API rejecting requests that don't include a page_size parameter
The API returning data in the wrong JSON format
A script calling the endpoint once, getting only the first page of results, and quietly treating that as the entire data set
questions.explain: Without following the pagination token, a script would only ever see the first page of results (e.g. 100 of 4,000 records) and silently miss the rest.

questions.q: What does an HTTP 429 response from an API indicate, and what should a well-behaved script do about it?
options: It indicates the requested resource does not exist; the script should log an error and continue
It indicates the OAuth2 token was invalid; the script should request a new client_id
It indicates the server crashed; the script should stop retrying immediately
It indicates the client exceeded its rate limit; the script should back off, ideally respecting a Retry-After header, before retrying
questions.explain: 429 Too Many Requests means the rate limit was exceeded. The lesson recommends exponential backoff, respecting a Retry-After header when the API provides one.

questions.q: In the exponential backoff example, what happens to the `delay` variable each time a 429 is received and no Retry-After header is present?
options: It decreases by half each retry
It doubles, so the wait time grows with each consecutive failed attempt
It resets to 1 second
It stays the same for every retry
questions.explain: The code sets delay *= 2 after each 429, meaning the fallback wait time doubles with each retry (1s, 2s, 4s, 8s...) when no Retry-After header is given.
